result.text:
401: Holding the history fixed gives a different comparison.  If the confidence
402: band is the only information supplied about the mean, reducing its upper
403: endpoint would exclude a mean that the band still allows.  Transport cannot
404: justify that reduction merely by expressing the same information in another
405: matrix.  This is a statement about widths on the same history, not about the
406: regret of policies that collect different histories.
407: 
408: \begin{proposition}[Reference-width floor on a fixed history]
409: \label{prop:reference-width-floor}
410: On the certificate event of \Cref{asm:abstract-transport}, every scored action
411: satisfies
412: \begin{equation}\label{eq:reference-width-floor}
413:  w_t^{\rm tr}(a):=e^{\bar D_t/2}\sqrt{\kappa_{+,t}}\hat s_t(a)
414:  \ge \bar s_t(a).
415: \end{equation}
416: For exact current widths, the actionwise multiplier
417: \begin{equation}\label{eq:actionwise-width-ratio}
418:  c_t(a)=\begin{cases}
419:  \bar s_t(a)/s_t(a),&\bq_t(a)\ne0,\\
420:  1,&\bq_t(a)=0
421:  \end{cases}
422:  \qquad\text{satisfies}\qquad c_t(a)s_t(a)=\bar s_t(a).
423: \end{equation}
424: Thus this exact actionwise correction reproduces the frozen-width score when
425: the center, radius, and bias are the same.
426: 
427: More generally, fix an action and $m_t(a)$, $b_t(a)$, $\beta_t>0$, and
428: $\bar s_t(a)$.  If the only restriction on its mean is the full interval
429: \eqref{eq:abstract-confidence-new}, a score
430: $m_t(a)+\beta_t w_t(a)+b_t(a)$ is an upper bound for every mean in that
431: interval if and only if $w_t(a)\ge\bar s_t(a)$.
432: \end{proposition}
433: 
434: The proposition's last statement treats the full interval supplied by one
435: confidence band as the set of possible means.  Additional restrictions on
436: the mean, a different center, or another simultaneous confidence event can
437: change that set.  The width floor concerns the information in that band.
438: 
439: The exact actionwise correction in \eqref{eq:actionwise-width-ratio}, including
440: its zero-query convention, reproduces the reference width.  An exact scalar
441: endpoint distance instead supplies a worst-direction multiplier, not
442: necessarily that actionwise equality.  Both comparisons hold on the same
443: history; they do not order the realized regret of policies whose actions and
444: subsequent histories differ.
445: 
446: The exact ratio also has a practical limitation: evaluating it as written in
447: \eqref{eq:actionwise-width-ratio} already uses the reference width that it
448: recovers.  It therefore supplies no computational shortcut as written.
449: This observation is not a general computational lower bound.
450: 
451: \begin{remark}[The reference band alone does not justify a smaller width]
452: \label{rem:naive-width-band-counterexample}
453: Consider an abstract confidence-band instance with $D>0$,
454: $\bVbar=\bI_2$, $\bV=\operatorname{diag}(e^D,e^{-D})$, and
455: $\bq=(1,0)^\top$.  Take $m=b=0$, $\beta>0$, and $\mu^*=\beta$.
456: Then $\bar s=1$ and $s=e^{-D/2}$, so
457: \[
458:  |\mu^*-m|=\beta\bar s+b,\qquad
459:  m+\beta s+b=\beta e^{-D/2}<\mu^*.
460: \]
461: Reference confidence therefore holds while the naive current-width score is
462: not an upper bound.  This illustrates the limited-information statement of
463: \Cref{prop:reference-width-floor}; it does not construct a realizable
464: scaled-tanh learning trajectory or establish that this certificate family was
465: necessary in the reported runs.
466: \end{remark}
467: 
468: \Cref{fig:transport-confidence-geometry} shows the illustrative slice
469: $D=\log 4$ and $\beta=1$.  The support of a metric unit ball in direction
470: $\bq$ is the corresponding inverse-metric width.  Here that support shrinks
471: under the current metric even though the reference confidence band still
472: allows its original upper endpoint.
473:

475:  \centering
476:  \input{figures/transport_conceptual_geometry.tex}
477:  \caption{Why the reference band alone does not justify a smaller current
478:  width.  In this abstract instance, the reference and current metric unit
479:  balls have different supports in the query direction.  With $D=\log4$,
480:  $m=b=0$ and $\beta=1$, the permitted mean $\mu^*=1$ exceeds the naive score
481:  $1/2$, whereas multiplying the current width by $e^{D/2}$ recovers the

488: For a finite list of actions, the general selector and measurability
489: requirements have a concrete implementation: evaluate the scores and choose
490: the first maximizer in a fixed ordering.  The following corollary records
491: the precise version used by finite-action policies.
492: 
493: \begin{corollary}[Measurably enumerated finite domains]
494: \label{cor:finite-enumeration-new}
495: Suppose there is a positive $\cHist_t^-$-measurable integer $K_t$ and
496: $\cHist_t^-$-measurable actions $a_{t,k}:\Omega\to\mathsf A$, $k\ge1$, such
497: that
498: \[
499:  \cA_t=\{a_{t,1},\ldots,a_{t,K_t}\}.
500: \]
501: If the learner chooses the smallest index attaining the score maximum, then the
502: selected action is $\cHist_t$-measurable and
503: \eqref{eq:approx-score-oracle-new} holds with $\xi_t=0$.  The score and
504: mean-reward suprema and the universal actionwise events reduce to measurable
505: finite maxima and intersections.  A fixed finite action set is the immediate
506: special case.
507: \end{corollary}
508: 
509: \paragraph{The order of a decision round.}
510: Algorithm~\ref{alg:transported-ucb} uses the corrected center constructed in
511: \Cref{sec:corrected-center}.  The learner forms and certifies its scores
512: before seeing the reward, selects an action, and only then updates the frozen
513: statistics.  This timing keeps the collection-time queries eligible for the
514: sequential confidence argument.  Selection and the regret analysis must use
515: the same computed width map, as the remark above emphasizes.
516: 
517: \begin{algorithm}[t]
518: \caption{Corrected-center specialization of transported UCB}\label{alg:transported-ucb}
519: \begin{algorithmic}[1]
520: \STATE Observe the context and graph-measurable action correspondence $\cA_t$; this defines $\cHist_t^-$.
521: \STATE Take the prefix-determined $\btheta_t$, $\bVbar_t$, and $\bV_t$; using the observed context, form $\bq_t(a)$, $m_t^{\rm corr}(a)$, and $b_t(a)$.
522: \STATE Choose $\cHist_t^-$-measurable failure budgets before their corresponding draws; reveal the pre-reward randomness $\Omega_t$.
523: \STATE Construct $\Calg_t$ and obtain pre-reward certificates $\bar D_t$, $\kappa_{-,t}$, and $\kappa_{+,t}$.
524: \STATE Obtain one jointly measurable solver upper-width map $\hat s_t(a)$ over the score domain.
525: \STATE Return a $\cHist_t$-measurable $\xi_t$-approximate selector for the score in \eqref{eq:transported-score-new}.
526: \STATE Observe the reward; update the frozen ridge estimator and \eqref{eq:reference-update-new}.
527: \end{algorithmic}
528: \end{algorithm}
529: 
530: The algorithm leaves the linear algebra implementation open.  Exact Cholesky
531: solves satisfy the solver conditions in exact arithmetic.  Conjugate gradient
532: (CG) can instead solve each action system using products with a fixed SPD
533: operator; a residual or energy argument must certify its returned widths.
534: Changing the matrix through a window, subsample, or sketch is a separate
535: approximation and requires an operator comparison.  The controlled experiment
536: in \Cref{sec:transport-followup} uses dense exact-current matrices and
537: Cholesky solves, so it does not evaluate these approximate or matrix-free paths.
538: 
539: \section{How to compare the frozen and current matrices}
540: \label{sec:logarithmic-transport}
541: 
542: The main theorem assumes a comparison between matrices.  This section explains
543: how to obtain one when past gradients are recomputed at the current parameter.
544: The matrix order $A\preceq B$ means that $B-A$ is positive semidefinite: the
545: quadratic form of $B$ is at least that of $A$ in every direction.  A two-sided
546: comparison therefore controls all query widths at once.
547: 
548: \paragraph{Measure relative change along a path.}
549: Imagine continuously changing the frozen matrix into the current matrix.
550: The path-length integrand below measures the largest relative change at each
551: point, after normalizing by the matrix there.  Integrating those changes gives
552: a multiplicative comparison between the endpoints.  The exponential form
553: allows large changes; it does not promise that the resulting factor is small.
554: 
555: \begin{lemma}[Logarithmic comparison along an SPD path]
556: \label{lem:log-spd-path}
557: Let $\bV:[0,1]\to\mathbb{S}_{++}^d$ be entrywise absolutely continuous and
558: let $\dot\bV(\tau)$ denote its almost-everywhere derivative.  If
559: \begin{equation}\label{eq:generic-path-length-new}
560:  \mathcal D(\bV)=\int_0^1
561:  \|\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\dot\bV(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}\,d\tau,
562: \end{equation}
563: then
564: \begin{equation}\label{eq:log-path-sandwich-new}
565:  e^{-\mathcal D(\bV)}\bV(0)\preceq\bV(1)
566:  \preceq e^{\mathcal D(\bV)}\bV(0).
567: \end{equation}
568: No commutativity or small-path assumption is required.
569: \end{lemma}
570: 
571: \begin{remark}[Thompson distance and selected-path length]
572: The integrand in \eqref{eq:generic-path-length-new} is the classical Thompson
573: Finsler norm on the positive-definite cone
574: \citep{thompson1963certain,nussbaum1994finsler}.  Its endpoint metric is
575: \[
576:  d_{\rm Th}(A,B)
577:  :=\inf\{r\ge0:e^{-r}A\preceq B\preceq e^rA\}.
578: \]
579: Equivalently,
580: \[
581:  d_{\rm Th}(A,B)
582:  =\left\|\log(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\right\|_{\rm op}.
583: \]
584: Therefore \Cref{lem:log-spd-path} gives
585: \begin{align*}
586:  d_{\rm Th}(\bV(0),\bV(1))&\le\mathcal D(\bV),\\
587:  d_{\rm Th}(\bVbar_t,\bV_t)&\le\mathcal D_t\le\bar D_t.
588: \end{align*}
589: The endpoint distance depends only on the two metrics, whereas
590: $\mathcal D(\bV)$ depends on the selected path.  The direct SPD path length is
591: independent of a factorization; the upper bound from
592: \Cref{lem:factor-spd-path} depends on the chosen factorization and interpolation.
593: \end{remark}
594: 
595: \begin{remark}[Sharpness of the symmetric exponential factors]
596: For $D\ge0$, let
597: \[
598: \begin{aligned}
599:  \bVbar&=\bI_2,&
600:  \bV&=\begin{pmatrix}e^D&0\\0&e^{-D}\end{pmatrix},\\
601:  \bV(\tau)&=\begin{pmatrix}e^{D\tau}&0\\0&e^{-D\tau}\end{pmatrix}.
602: \end{aligned}
603: \]
604: Then
605: \[
606:  \bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\dot\bV(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}
607:  =\begin{pmatrix}D&0\\0&-D\end{pmatrix},
608: \]
609: so $\mathcal D(\bV)=d_{\rm Th}(\bVbar,\bV)=D$.  For $q_1=e_1$,
610: $\bar s(q_1)=1$ and $s(q_1)=e^{-D/2}$, so
611: $\bar s=e^{D/2}s$ is attained.  For $q_2=e_2$,
612: $s(q_2)=e^{D/2}$ and $\bar s(q_2)=1$, so
613: $s=e^{D/2}\bar s$ is attained.  Thus each one-way factor is sharp, and a
614: uniform argument based only on the symmetric Thompson-distance bound cannot
615: improve the resulting round-trip factor $e^D$.  This is a metric-factor
616: sharpness statement, not a contextual-bandit regret lower bound and not a
617: claim that every trajectory attains the worst case.
618: \end{remark}
619: 
620: \paragraph{Work with the gradients that form the matrix.}
621: A replay matrix is a ridge term plus a Gram matrix of gradient features.
622: Stack those features as rows of $\Bmat$.  It is often easier to bound how
623: these rows change than to analyze the full SPD path directly.  The next lemma
624: turns a bound on the changing factor into a bound on matrix path length.
625: Its normalization by $\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}$ retains information about which
626: directions the data have already constrained.
627: 
628: \begin{lemma}[Rectangular factor-path certificate]
629: \label{lem:factor-spd-path}
630: Let $\Bmat:[0,1]\to\R^{m\times d}$ be absolutely continuous and set
631: $\bV(\tau)=\lambda\bI+\Bmat(\tau)^\top\Bmat(\tau)$, with $\lambda>0$.
632: Then
633: \begin{equation}\label{eq:factor-path-bound-new}
634:  \mathcal D(\bV)\le2\int_0^1
635:  \|\dot\Bmat(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}\,d\tau.
636: \end{equation}
637: More generally, suppose there is a measurable function
638: $\nu_t:[0,1]\to[0,\infty)$ with $\nu_t\in L^1([0,1])$ such that
639: \[
640:  \dot\Bmat(\tau)^\top\dot\Bmat(\tau)
641:  \preceq\nu_t(\tau)^2\bV(\tau)
642: \]
643: almost everywhere.  Then
644: $\mathcal D(\bV)\le2\int_0^1\nu_t(\tau)d\tau$.  For nonnegative $\nu_t$, the
645: displayed PSD premise is equivalently the norm condition
646: $\|\dot\Bmat(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}\le\nu_t(\tau)$ almost everywhere.
647: \end{lemma}
648: 
649: For a scalar prediction, each past observation contributes a gradient row.
650: Move that row from its collection-time parameter $\btheta_s$ to the current
651: parameter $\btheta_t$ along its own straight segment.  The $s$th row is
652: \begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-factor-path-new}
653:  \sigma^{-1}\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_s+
654:  \tau(\btheta_t-\btheta_s)}(x_s,a_s)^\top.
655: \end{equation}
656: The endpoint matrices are the frozen and exact current matrices.  The path
657: between them is a device for comparing those endpoints: different rows begin
658: at different collection-time parameters.  It need not be the generalized
659: Gauss--Newton (GGN) matrix of any common intermediate model, and it is not the
660: learner's training trajectory.
661: A weighted or heteroscedastic squared loss uses row
662: $\sqrt{w_s}\,\nabla\mu^\top$ for a nonnegative collection-time weight $w_s$
663: fixed before the corresponding reward.
664: If the weight is fixed along the interpolation, the same proof only rescales
665: the corresponding row.  If it changes with the path, the derivative of
666: $\sqrt{w_s(\tau)}$ is an additional obligation.
667: 
668: \paragraph{A certificate from smoothness and parameter movement.}
669: A prediction-Hessian bound controls how fast each gradient can change along
670: its segment.  Combined with the ridge lower bound on the matrix, it gives a
671: certificate in terms of $Q_t$, the accumulated squared distances from the
672: current parameter to collection-time parameters.  This route is easy to state,
673: but it can discard information about well-constrained directions.
674: 
675: \begin{corollary}[Hessian path certificate]
676: \label{cor:hessian-path-new}
677: Suppose the parameter region is convex and
678: $\|\nabla_\theta^2\mu_\theta(x_s,a_s)\|_{\rm op}\le L_g$ along every segment
679: in \eqref{eq:scalar-factor-path-new}.  With
680: \begin{equation}\label{eq:Qt-new}
681:  Q_t=\sum_{s<t}\|\btheta_t-\btheta_s\|_2^2,
682: \end{equation}
683: the exact current and frozen metrics satisfy
684: \begin{equation}\label{eq:hessian-path-sandwich-new}
685:  e^{-\bar D_t}\bVbar_t\preceq\bV_t\preceq e^{\bar D_t}\bVbar_t,
686:  \qquad
687:  \bar D_t=\frac{2L_g\sqrt{Q_t}}{\sigma\sqrt\lambda}.
688: \end{equation}
689: This remains valid when $\bar D_t\ge1$.  At $t=1$, the factor has zero rows,
690: $Q_1=0$, and both metrics equal $\lambda\bI$.
691: \end{corollary}
692: 
693: The relative condition in \Cref{lem:factor-spd-path} retains that directional
694: information and can be much sharper than the ridge-only Hessian bound.
695: Changes in directions with larger matrix eigenvalues are downweighted by
696: the inverse-matrix normalization.  Both constructions permit gradient
697: rotation; the factor-path lemma requires neither a fixed subspace nor known
698: rank.
699: 
700: \paragraph{Convert matrix comparisons into width comparisons.}
701: The next proposition gives the outward and return comparisons used in the
702: regret theorem.  It also shows how a relative-error bound for an approximate
703: operator supplies the factors $\kappa_{-,t}$ and $\kappa_{+,t}$.
704: 
705: \begin{proposition}[Width transport and approximate operators]
706: \label{prop:width-transport-new}
707: Under \eqref{eq:path-length-new} and \eqref{eq:operator-sandwich-new},
708: \begin{align}
709:  \bar s_t^2(a)&\le e^{\bar D_t}\kappa_{+,t}s_{\Calg,t}^2(a),
710:  &s_{\Calg,t}^2(a)&\le
711:  e^{\bar D_t}\kappa_{-,t}^{-1}\bar s_t^2(a).
712:  \label{eq:two-way-width-new}
713: \end{align}
714: Exact current curvature has $\kappa_{-,t}=\kappa_{+,t}=1$.  More generally,
715: the operational relative-error certificate
716: \begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-operator-certificate-new}
717:  \|\bV_t^{-1/2}(\Calg_t-\bV_t)\bV_t^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}
718:  \le\varepsilon_t<1
719: \end{equation}
720: gives $\kappa_{-,t}=1-\varepsilon_t$ and
721: $\kappa_{+,t}=1+\varepsilon_t$.  An upper comparison alone does not imply a
722: lower factor.
723: \end{proposition}
724: 
725: \paragraph{Compare the endpoints directly when possible.}
726: Following an entire path is not required if a valid two-sided comparison of
727: the endpoint matrices is already available.  The next corollary inserts that
728: comparison into the same confidence and regret argument.  Its upper factor
729: protects optimism; its lower factor supplies the return comparison, so their
730: ratio enters the regret bound.
731: 
732: \begin{corollary}[Direct endpoint sandwich]
733: \label{cor:relative-endpoint-ucb}
734: Replace the path premise \eqref{eq:path-length-new} in
735: \Cref{thm:transported-ucb} by pre-reward measurable factors that, on the joint
736: certificate event, satisfy
737: \begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-endpoint-sandwich}
738:  0<c_{-,t}\le c_{+,t}<\infty,\qquad
739:  c_{-,t}\bVbar_t\preceq\bV_t\preceq c_{+,t}\bVbar_t.
740: \end{equation}
741: Replace \eqref{eq:transported-score-new} by the score
742: \begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-endpoint-score}
743:  U_t^{\rm rel}(a)=m_t(a)+\beta_t\sqrt{c_{+,t}\kappa_{+,t}}
744:  \hat s_t(a)+b_t(a),
745: \end{equation}
746: and require the same finite measurable supremum and approximate-selector
747: condition for this score.  Keep every other hypothesis of that theorem.
748: On the joint confidence and certificate event, writing
749: $h_t=1+\alpha_t\sqrt{c_{+,t}\kappa_{+,t}/(c_{-,t}\kappa_{-,t})}$,
750: \begin{align}
751:  \operatorname{reg}_t
752:  &\le\beta_t h_t\bar s_t(a_t)+2b_t(a_t)+\xi_t,\nonumber\\
753:  R_T&\le\sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)
754:  \gamma_T\sum_{t=1}^T\beta_t^2h_t^2}
755:  +2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t.
756:  \label{eq:relative-endpoint-regret}
757: \end{align}
758: The probability statement of \Cref{thm:transported-ucb} is unchanged, with
759: the endpoint certificate included in its joint certificate event.
760: \end{corollary}
761: 
762: This result uses the endpoint matrices directly.  In particular,
763: $\max\{-\log c_{-,t},\log c_{+,t}\}$ bounds their Thompson distance;
764: it need not bound the length of the synthetic path
765: \eqref{eq:scalar-factor-path-new}.  Its effective width still obeys the
766: reference-width floor: $\sqrt{c_{+,t}\kappa_{+,t}}\hat s_t(a)\ge\bar s_t(a)$.
767: 
768: \paragraph{What extends to vector outputs?}
769: The factor construction also accommodates several output coordinates and
770: weights, provided their changes are controlled as well.  For vector outputs,
771: let $J_s(\theta)\in\R^{p_s\times d}$ and supply an
772: absolutely continuous factor $R_s(\theta)\in\R^{r_s\times p_s}$ satisfying
773: $R_s^\top R_s=W_s\succeq0$.  Stacking
774: $B_s=R_sJ_s\in\R^{r_s\times d}$ gives
775: $\lambda I+\sum_sJ_s^\top W_sJ_s$.  Along a path,
776: $\dot B_s=\dot R_sJ_s+R_s\dot J_s$; both terms must be controlled.  This
777: covers the geometry of weighted Fisher/GGN factors but does not by itself prove
778: a likelihood confidence sequence or an exponential-family regret theorem.
779: 
780: \section{A confidence center that does not require optimizer convergence}
781: \label{sec:corrected-center}
782: 
783: So far, the confidence band has been an assumption.  We now construct one
784: for squared loss.  The difficulty is that an arbitrarily trained nonlinear
785: predictor need not be the center of a valid confidence band.  The construction
786: uses that predictor as an anchor, then corrects it using a linear estimate
787: formed from collection-time features.  Confidence comes from this frozen
788: linear estimation problem; it does not require the nonlinear optimizer to
789: have converged.
790: 
791: There is a cost to this separation.  Linearizing the model introduces Taylor
792: error, and the reference model may not exactly represent the true mean.
793: The resulting band must account for both errors, in past observations and in
794: the current prediction.  The assumptions below make these costs explicit.
795: 
796: \paragraph{Noise and the reference model.}
797: Let $\sigma>0$ and let the reward obey
798: $r_t=\mu_t^*(a_t)+\eta_t$, where, for every $u\in\R$,
799: \begin{equation}\label{eq:new-noise-condition}
800:  \mathbb E[\exp(u\eta_t)\mid\cHist_t]
